# strict-spec-driven
English | 中文
**Documentation:** Quick Start · Architecture · Architecture Quickstart · UI Design Quickstart · Roa
dmap Quick Start · Roadmap Guide · AGENTS
`strict-spec-driven` is a YAML-first spec-driven development workflow. It provides the spec-driven l
ifecycle (propose → apply → verify → skill-driven code review → archive) with Agent Skills integrati
on, converting workflow artifacts — specs, changes, roadmap, tasks, questions — into strict YAML sch
emas enforced by deterministic scripts.
`SKILL.md` files remain Markdown because that is the Agent Skills packaging format requirement. What
changes is the artifact format those skills generate and consume.

Preferred standalone roadmap work-item files |

ec files |

ckages (`strict-spec-*` and `strict-roadmap-*`) |

This repository keeps a single active workflow directory, `.strict-spec-driven/`. A `.spec-driven/`
directory is only relevant as migration *input* for other projects that still use the legacy Markdow
n workflow — see Migration Boundaries. This repository completed that migration and retains no root
`.spec-driven/` directory.

## Requirement Interrogation

Every path that starts from a human request — `/strict-spec-brainstorm`,
`/strict-spec-propose`, `/s

trict-spec-bugfix`, `/strict-spec-auto` — interrogates
the *need* before the change-intake gate inte

rrogates the *solution*. It runs
first because a well-scoped change built against a misread need is

still the
wrong change.

Requirement answers are never taken from repository evidence. Code shows what
the system does; it ca

nnot show what a person wants. Only the requester's own
words — including what they already said in

the request — or replayed roadmap
planned-change and milestone detail may answer them.

The first `generate <change-name> questions ...` invocation seeds five canonical
questions into `que

stions.yaml` as open entries, so a newly authored change is
blocked until they are answered:
| Question id | Asks | A sufficient answer contains |
| `requirement-problem` | What is concretely going wrong today, and for whom? | Who is affected, wha

t they do today instead, and how often — without naming a feature |
| `requirement-outcome` | What o
bservable difference proves it is solved? | What a person will see or no longer have to do, checkabl

e from outside the system |
| `requirement-trigger` | Why now — what forced this? | The concrete eve

nt, deadline, incident, or cost, or an honest statement that nothing forced it |
| `requirement-non-
goals` | What must explicitly not change? | The nearby behavior that must survive untouched, and who

relies on it |
| `requirement-interpretation` | Which reading is intended? | The intended reading s
tated plainly enough to rule the others out |

Each seeded entry carries its own explanation — why it is asked, what a
sufficient answer contains,

a worked example, and what the answer changes — so
answering does not require prior knowledge of thi

ample, and what the answer changes — so
answering does not require prior knowledge of this workflow.

Answers are recorded with attribution. `--answered-by human` and
`--answered-by roadmap` satisfy the

gate; `--answered-by assumption` records
that the agent supplied the answer without human confirmat

ion and blocks `ready`
until a human decides:

## Scene-First Requirement Routing

Requirement interrogation establishes the *need*. Scene-first routing
establishes the *situation the

need occurs in*, and it runs between the two
gates above and below, because a requirement set writt

en without it has holes
that are invisible in the requirements themselves.

`/strict-spec-propose`, `/strict-spec-brainstorm`, and `/strict-spec-auto` ask
four questions in eve

ry proposal, whatever the change turns out to be: who acts
and what each actor does, what must alrea

dy be true before the main flow begins,
what happens step by ordered step when nothing goes wrong, a

nd what can go
wrong, what triggers each exception flow, and what happens then. An author asked
for

requirements immediately skips all four and never notices, because nothing
in a requirement records
the question that was never asked.

The scene is **mandatory as a question and optional as an artifact**. When the
change touches user-o

bservable behavior, the scene is written down — as a delta
scene under the change, before the delta

spec, so each requirement is derived
from a flow step rather than recalled. When the change is purel

y technical
— a refactor, build or test tooling, repository maintenance, an architecture
constraint,

a script, or skill guidance — there is no actor flow to describe,
and the skill records why no scen
e applies instead of inventing one.

Every flow step declares either the requirements that cover it or an explicit
reason it is deliberat

ely covered by none, and one step may name covering
requirements across several spec areas. Once a c

hange carries a delta scene,
`ready` and `verify` exit non-zero on a step naming neither, and the di

agnostic
names the runnable command that records the coverage:

spec. A project that re

cords no scene sees no new diagnostic and no new required
field, so adopting scenes is incremental a

nd upgrading the CLI is not a breaking
change. Scenes live under `.strict-spec-driven/scenes/<area>/
